Part of the Historian’s job is to determine if a
structure slated for demolition is historic in nature
and if so, what (if anything) should or might happen
with regard to possibly saving the structure. The
Historian’s Office has no authority to prevent a dem-
olition. At the very least, structures may be photo-
graphically documented inside and out, and when
possible, architectural elements of the structure can
be saved. Saving architectural elements involves
suggesting the property owner or demolition compa-
ny collaborate with the Historic Albany Founda-
tion’s Parts Warehouse whose volunteers salvage
architectural elements inside and outside of a struc-
ture. The items salvaged by the Historic Albany
Foundation are for sale in their warehouse to those
who are restoring an older home and looking for a
certain architectural piece not found elsewhere. The
Historic Albany Foundation is a non-profit organiza-
tion and items donated to them are tax deductible as
allowed by law. The process saves important archi-
tectural pieces, lessens the amount of debris going
into a landfill, and provides the property owner a
deduction for tax purposes.
In the case of 4 Kraft Avenue, the address did not
raise any flags with me. I checked the list of proper-
ties included in the 1980’s Historic Resource Survey
of buildings within the Town, and 4 Kraft Avenue
was never surveyed. A check with the Assessor’s
Office files indicated that the “probable” construc-
tion date of the building was about 1930.

I went to Google Earth and the address in question
was hard to see from trees that surrounded it, so a
personal inspection of 4 Kraft Avenue was in order.
At first, the location was hard to pin down along
Kraft Avenue until I pulled into the west entrance of
the parking lot for the old Sunset Bowling Alley of
1160 Central Avenue. There, hidden from view of
Central Avenue and somewhat secluded from Kraft
Avenue itself was an old home on a small lot shaded
in front by two mature maple trees. The house was
vacant and open and in the stages of being prepped
for demolition. All of its windows had been re-
moved. The modern yellow vinyl siding that once
wrapped the exterior walls had all been stripped off
and thrown inside as part of what would become the
demolition debris. The tarpaper used to seal the
house during the time the Vinyl siding was initially
installed remained on most of the home’s old clap-
board exterior walls.
I am not a professional architectural historian, but
something told me that this home was far older than
the circa 1930 date listed in the Assessor’s records.
Several things puzzled me. The rear of the house,
not the front, faced Kraft Avenue, the front of the
home faced east, its main entrance was clearly origi-
nal to the home, having many layers of paint cover-
ing the ornate trim around the pillared entrance door
surrounded on both sides by vertical window lights
and a large rectangular window above the entry
door. An ornate zipper like pattern of trim was im-
mediately above the entry door. Metal script let-
ters above the door read “Eleven Sixty” and the
numbers 1160 were on the door itself. Below the
numbers on the door was a quaint metal casting of a
trotting horse with driver seated in a four-wheeled
buggy, possibly another hint to the age of the house.
The front door was wide open and I peered in. The
first thing I saw was a robust Newell Post and intact
staircase and railing leading to the second floor.
Certainly, this Newell Post and the architecture of
the front door with a massive lock plate (very simi-
lar to one on the front door of the circa 1830 Pruyn
House of Colonie) pre-dated the 1930 date suggest-
ed on the document in the Assessor’s Office. I
snapped a photo of the Newell Post and staircase
and sent it to Mr. Walter Wheeler, Architectural
Historian expert at Hartgen Archaeology at Albany.

Sarah graduated as M.D. in
1877. She became an instructor
in the field of gynecology, an
assistant to the chair of general
surgery and an instructor of sur-
gery, specializing in the diseas-
es of women and children. At
that time “there was not in all
New York, a single ward in any
hospital devoted exclusively to
children under two years of
age.”
In 1888, the Babies Hospital of New York opened with
Doctors Julia and Sarah McNutt as attending physicians.
Dr. Julia McNutt founded the Post Graduate Training
School for Nurses, an organization incorporated by her
sister Dr. Sarah McNutt. The number of medical socie-
ties, journals, and authors of articles of medical diseases
and treatments written by both doctors are too many to
include in this writing. Dr. Julia was also involved in
many other societies, having founded the Albany Colony
of The Society of New England Women who often met
at the McNutt home on Central Avenue. She also led a
contingent of professional women who marched in a
Women’s Suffrage event at Albany in 1917. The sever-
al articles about Doctors Julia and Sarah McNutt found
on the Old Fulton Post Cards web page reveal that their
home was often the site of hosting different social
events. One article described the home as filled with
fine antique New England furniture pieces. The sisters
lovingly referred to their home as “The Nutshell”.
A March 2, 1927 Albany Times Union newspaper article
interviewed Dr. Julia McNutt on her 83rd birthday. It
described her as an Albany pioneer physician who re-
called the days when she was the only woman doctor in
Albany. Dr. Julia said, “When I received my degree,
[and here her undimmed eyes smiled] and came to Alba-
ny to practice, I sent out my announcement to the profes-
sion. I got complete silence, except from Dr. Vander-
Veer, who wrote me a fine letter of welcome and encour-
agement, assuring me that I was needed and that I would
have a chance for service here where there were no
women doctors.”
Dr. Julia also remarked that she “liked the modern
world” but would not have a radio for fear that “it would
be going all the time.” Her values rested more with
reading because she could “pick and choose her enter-
tainment” such as a good detective story, but anything
“as long as it’s a good story” and pleasing to her.
Note: Julia died on Dec. 14, 1928 in Colonie. Her sister
Sarah died Sept. 10, 1930 in Colonie. Both are interred
in the McNutt family plot in the Albany Rural Cemetery.
